hints: Start by looking for the word budding in Fig. 2.1. Budding makes a genetically identical copy of the parent nucleus, so which type of nuclear division must that be?
Look at stage 4 where one diploid a-alpha cell becomes four haploid spores in an ascus. A change from diploid to haploid to make four different cells points to which type of division?
Think about when new combinations of a and alpha genetic material are first brought together and then reshuffled. Which stages bring two types together or halve and remix chromosomes?
Count the symbols inside each cell. A single a or single alpha means one set of chromosomes, while a-alpha together in one cell means two sets. Which stages never show a-alpha together?
Now find the loop where every cell shown contains both a and alpha together and only multiplies by budding. Which numbered cycle fits that?
walkthrough:
Link Budding to Mitosis**
Budding produces a daughter cell with a copy of the parent nucleus, so it is asexual reproduction by mitosis. In Fig. 2.1 budding is labelled in stage 1 for haploid a and haploid alpha cells and in stage 3 for diploid a-alpha cells. So stages 1 and 3 involve mitosis.

Link Spore Formation to Meiosis**
Stage 4 shows one diploid a-alpha cell producing an ascus containing four haploid spores, two a and two alpha. Reduction from diploid to haploid to make four genetically different products is meiosis. So stage 4 involves meiosis.

Spot Where Variation Arises**
New genetic variation arises when genomes combine and when meiosis reshuffles them. Stage 2 is mating and formation of the zygote, bringing a and alpha together, and stage 4 is meiosis with crossing over and independent assortment. So stages 2 and 4 produce new genetic variation.

Check Ploidy in Each Stage**
Haploid means one mating-type symbol per cell. Stage 1 loops contain only single a or single alpha cells. Stage 5 arrows show spores germinating back into haploid a and alpha cycles, so only haploid cells are shown. Stage 3 loop contains only double a-alpha cells, so only diploid cells are shown.
Final answer: involve mitosis: 1 and 3; involve meiosis: 4; produces new genetic variation: 2 and 4; shows only haploid cells: 1 and 5; shows only diploid cells: 3

hints: Look at what stage 4 starts with and ends with - one diploid cell to four haploid spores. Is that the asexual budding pattern or the sexual pattern?
Recall the two main ways meiosis shuffles alleles between chromosomes and between daughter cells.
Think about why being all genetically identical is risky if nutrients, temperature or other conditions change suddenly.
Consider the extra clues in the stem: spores made when nutrients lack and germinate only when conditions improve, plus the mating of different types in Fig. 2.1.
walkthrough:
Identify the Type of Reproduction**
Stage 3 cells are diploid and divide by budding, which is asexual and makes clones. When nutrients run out they enter stage 4 and form four haploid spores by meiosis. That is sexual reproduction because it involves reduction division and later mating of different types.

Explain How Variation Is Created**
During meiosis, crossing over exchanges alleles between homologous chromosomes and independent assortment shuffles whole chromosomes into spores. Then in stage 2, haploid a and haploid alpha cells mate at random, so fertilisation fuses random combinations of gametes. Together this creates many different allele combinations.

Link Variation to Survival**
In a changing environment the optimum phenotype changes. A clonal population may all be poorly adapted and all die. With sexual variation, at least some spores are likely to carry an advantageous combination of alleles, so some survive and continue the population.

Add the Spore Survival Advantage**
Spores are resistant and dormant. They do not germinate until conditions have improved, so the varied offspring wait out the harsh period. The life cycle can also switch back to rapid asexual budding in stages 1 and 3 when conditions are good.

Final answer: Stage 4 is sexual reproduction by meiosis; produces genetic variation due to crossing over and independent assortment and random mating / fusion of gametes; some spores have advantageous combinations of alleles so are adapted to survive changing environment and avoid whole population being wiped out; spores remain dormant until conditions improve.

hints: Think about how many copies of each gene a haploid cell carries, so can a recessive allele ever hide behind another copy?
In an asexually reproducing haploid population, if one cell gains a new mutation and makes clones, which cells carry the mutation?
Now think about a diploid cell with one normal dominant allele and one new harmful recessive allele. Will the harmful phenotype show in a heterozygote?
walkthrough:
Reason With Haploid Genetics**
A haploid cell has only one allele for each gene, so there is no second copy to mask anything. Every allele present is expressed. A new harmful recessive mutation will therefore show its harmful effect immediately in that cell.

Scale Up to the Haploid Population**
Asexual reproduction by mitosis makes clones, so the mutation is passed only to the direct descendants of that one mutated cell. Only that clone is affected and may die. All other independent haploid lines never received the mutation, so the population as a whole continues unaffected and the mutated allele is removed when that line dies.

Reason With Diploid Genetics**
A diploid cell has two alleles. If the new harmful mutation is recessive, a heterozygote has one normal dominant allele and one mutant recessive allele. The dominant normal allele masks the recessive allele, so the harmful phenotype is not expressed and the cell functions normally.

Final answer: haploid population: only the cell with the harmful mutation is affected and may die, rest of population unaffected and mutation is removed with that cell; diploid population: harmful recessive allele is masked by dominant normal allele and not expressed in heterozygote, so no damaging effect.

hints: Start with cell structure and nutrition. How do fungi obtain food compared with plants, and what type of cells do they have compared with bacteria?
Think about the material in their walls and the thread-like body form, which are different from plants and animals.
walkthrough:
Recall Core Fungal Biology**
Fungi are eukaryotes with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. They are heterotrophs that feed saprotrophically on dead organic matter or parasitically on living hosts, digesting food externally and absorbing the products.

Add Structural Features**
Unlike plants which have cellulose walls, fungi have walls made of chitin. Most form thread-like hyphae grouped into a mycelium, often with multinucleate cytoplasm. The kingdom includes both unicellular forms like yeast and multicellular forms like mushrooms.

Final answer: Any two from: eukaryotic cells; heterotrophic / saprotrophic / parasitic nutrition by extracellular digestion; cell walls made of chitin; hyphae / mycelium; multinucleate cells; includes both unicellular and multicellular forms.
